extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology/literary theory and advanced writers studying point of view
extracted.subtask_description: A focused study of narrative focalization: identifying types (nonfocalized, internal — fixed/variable/multiple — external), how focalization operates locally vs globally, permissible alterations (paralipsis/paralepsis), and diagnostic tests (Barthes' first-person test, modalizing locutions, perceptual restriction). Useful for literary analysis and for applying point-of-view choices in fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focalization (general concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the abstract term 'focalization' to replace the specifically visual connotations of 'vision, field, and point of view'; corresponds to 'focus of narration.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat focalization as the narrative restriction or distribution of information (the field through which events are perceived), distinct from pure narrator voice or grammatical person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonfocalized narrative (zero focalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative with zero focalization — the classical omniscient narrative in which there is no specific restriction of field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identified by the absence of a stable focal character through whom perceptions are filtered; can nonetheless be analyzed as multifocalized ad libitum (i.e., capable of simulating focalization as needed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal focalization (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative in which perception, thought, or point of view is presented through a character's consciousness (focal character).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be realized strictly (never refer to the character from outside, never analyze his thoughts objectively) or in a less strict, practical sense (see Barthes' criterion). Examples: The Ambassadors, What Maisie Knew.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed internal focalization
rubrics_metrics.description: A subtype of internal focalization where the narrative consistently passes through a single character (everything passes through Strether in The Ambassadors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produces sustained restriction of information and a consistent field of perception across the focalized sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable internal focalization
rubrics_metrics.description: A subtype where the focal character changes over the course of the narrative or across sections (e.g., Madame Bovary: focal character moves from Charles to Emma to Charles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be rapid and elusive (as in Stendhal) and need not apply to an entire work — often operates at the level of sections or scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple internal focalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Many distinct characters supply focal perspectives on the same events (e.g., epistolary novels or Browning's The Ring and the Book; cinematic analogue: Rashomon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows the same event to be evoked several times from different subjective points of view; useful for polyphonic or relativized truth effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: External focalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative focalization that remains outside characters' consciousnesses; the hero performs without access to his thoughts or feelings (author/narrator withholds interiority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in detective, adventure, and enigmatic openings (Hammett, Hemingway, Scott, Verne, Dumas, Balzac). External focalization can intentionally create mystery or riddle-like effects by withholding inner states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local rather than global application of focalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Focalization need not be steady over a whole work; single focalization formulas often bear only on definite narrative sections (which can be very short).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate focalization at the level of narrative sections/scenes rather than assuming a single mode for an entire book; look for shifts and mixtures (external scenes within an internally focalized novel, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversibility and ambiguity between external/internal focalization
rubrics_metrics.description: External focalization with respect to one character may be equivalent to internal focalization through another; similarly, nonfocalized narrative can often be analyzed as multifocalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of simple labels; analyze whose perceptions are being privileged and whether ambiguity arises from role/status (e.g., hero vs witness) rather than pure mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous vs pragmatic internal focalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Strict internal focalization would forbid any external description of the focal character or objective analysis of his thoughts; in practice, internal focalization is often applied less rigidly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess passages for objective narrative intrusions (narrator telling what a character 'does and thinks') versus passages that confine themselves to what the character actually perceives ('vision with').

rubrics_metrics.name: Barthes' first‑person test for internal focalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical minimal criterion: a narrative section belongs to internal focalization if it can be rewritten into the first person without changing the discourse other than pronouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this test diagnostically: sentences that translate cleanly to 'I saw...' indicate internal focalization, while sentences asserting inaccessible inner states ('the tinkling ... seemed to awaken in Bond a sudden inspiration') indicate external focalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between focalizing and narrating instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when narrator and hero are the same person (first person), the narrating instance usually 'knows' more than the hero did and thus narrating personhood does not equal focalization through the hero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate the narrator's present knowledge from the hero's momentary ignorance when diagnosing focalization; first-person narration can include narrator's retrospective interventions that exceed hero's original field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alterations (isolated infractions of focalization code)
rubrics_metrics.description: Isolated changes in focalization that function as 'alterations' analogous to musical modulation; two kinds: giving less information than principle requires (paralipsis) or giving more (paralepsis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat isolated deviations as local rhetorical/poetic effects rather than wholesale incoherence; analyze whether the dominant mode/mood remains intelligible despite the alteration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paralipsis (lateral omission)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate omission of information the hero and narrator both know — withholding an important action or thought from the reader while remaining within internal focalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to produce surprise or preserve mystery (Stendhal's concealment of Octave's impotence; detective-story techniques of hiding the murderer's memory). Evaluate whether omission is rhetorically justified or produces a paradoxical 'cheating'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paralepsis (excess information)
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving information that exceeds what the governing code of focalization authorizes — e.g., an inroad into a character's consciousness during an otherwise external focalization, or incidental access to another character's thoughts in internal focalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify transitions where external narration slips into interior access (Peau de chagrin examples) or passages where the narrator supplies other characters' private thoughts (Maisie & Mrs. Farange). Consider whether paralepsis signals a gradual shift of mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indices vs explicit information — reader inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative often 'says less than it knows' but supplies indices that invite reader interpretation (Barthes' indices); reader interprets behavior from signs even in external focalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between explicit narrative information and implicit indices (gestures, looks, physical signs) that the informed reader decodes; consider how this gap between said and known shapes irony, suspense, and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modalizing locutions as focalization alibis/indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Modal words and locutions (perhaps, as if, seem, appear) allow the narrator to state hypothetically what he cannot assert without stepping outside internal focalization; they function both as 'alibis' and as indicators of focalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note frequency and multiplicity of such hypotheses: many 'perhaps' clauses often indicate the narrator's (or hero's) uncertainty rather than genuine authorial knowledge, and the plurality of options tends to reinforce insolubility rather than supply hidden truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polymodality / narrator-hero oneness and its effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The coincidence of narrator and hero (autobiographical/first-person framing) does not automatically produce focalization through the hero; autobiographical narrators are more 'authorized' to speak and therefore may intermix narrator-knowledge with hero-ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate focalization in autobiographical narratives by separating the narrator's present information from the hero's contemporaneous perceptions; the autobiographical narrator may choose to practice paralipsis (suppressing later knowledge) or not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proustian rule for focalized description (perceptual restriction & duration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proustian descriptions are rigorously focalized: their 'duration' never exceeds that of real contemplation, and their content never exceeds what is actually perceived by the contemplator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analysis or emulation, ensure that focalized descriptive passages limit themselves to the perceivable details available to the focal consciousness and respect temporal plausibility of perception (scenes often end when perception ends).

rubrics_metrics.name: Focalization as tool for character opacity ('creature in flight')
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematically adopting the point of view of one protagonist permits the author to leave the feelings of other characters almost completely in shadow, creating enigmatic or 'fugitive' characters (Proust's 'creature in flight').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sustained internal focalization to produce subjectivity of love, ambiguity of other minds, and delayed revelation; recognize how this choice shapes reader empathy and narrative mystery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focalization and the topos of initial ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors often feign ignorance at the narrative opening ('the author pretends not to know him') as a ritual to introduce a character; this initial ignorance may be quickly resolved or deliberately prolonged for effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing openings, look for this device as a conventional way of staging introduction and managing narrative knowledge; it can legitimize later shifts from external to internal perspectives.
